source.title: Signs of Dehydration in Infants & Children

notes: AAP dehydration page lists 'fewer than six wet diapers per day' as a sign of mild-moderate dehydration in infants, alongside dry mouth, fewer tears, sunken soft spot. Page last updated 2019. source.title: Signs of Dehydration in Infants & Children

notes: AAP: urinating only one to two times per day is a sign of severe dehydration (with excessive sleepiness, sunken eyes, cool discolored hands and feet). Flags at 2 or fewer (inclusive). The source counts urinations; the app counts logged wet diapers, which can undercount (one diaper may hold several voids), so the copy must say 'wet diapers logged' and missing logs give 'not enough data', never a count of zero. The source is a general child dehydration page, not a neonatal rule; applying it from day 5 is this file's choice. Population: healthy term infants. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Baby's First Days: Bowel Movements & Urination

source.title: Baby's First Days: Bowel Movements & Urination

source.title: How to change your baby's nappy

notes: NHS: meconium is passed during or after birth, 'or some time in the first 48 hours'. No first stool by 48 h -> flag. Population: healthy term infants (any feeding method unless stated). Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: ABM Clinical Protocol #3: Supplementary Feedings in the Healthy Term Breastfed Neonate, Revised 2017 (Breastfeed Med 2017;12:188-198, PMID 28294631)

Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: The Many Colors of Baby Poop

notes: AAP: 'White poop is quite rare but needs to be brought to the attention of a doctor as soon as possible.' NIDDK: infants with biliary atresia may have pale yellow, gray, or white stools; AAP biliary atresia page: jaundice and pale stools develop by 4-6 weeks. NHS: pale creamy poo in a baby over 24 h old -> urgent GP/111; keep a sample. Matches stool-card colors 1-3 (acholic). Any single occurrence should prompt contacting the pediatrician promptly. Population: healthy term infants (any feeding method unless stated). Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Stools - Unusual Color (symptom checker, Schmitt Pediatric Guidelines)

source.title: Breast-Feeding Questions (symptom checker, Schmitt Pediatric Guidelines)

source.title: The Many Colors of Baby Poop

source.title: Faltering growth: recognition and management of faltering growth in children (NG75)

source.title: ABM Clinical Protocol #3: Supplementary Feedings in the Healthy Term Breastfed Neonate, Revised 2017 (Breastfeed Med 2017;12:188-198, PMID 28294631)

source.title: First Office Visit (3-5 Days)

notes: AAP: 'Birth weight will likely not be regained until 7 to 14 days after birth, particularly for breastfed newborns'. Soft flag. Metric: the baby's age in completed days while no weight recorded since birth has reached birth weight. Flags at 14 completed days or more (op gte). Once any weight at or above birth weight is recorded the metric is undefined and the rule does not fire, even if a later weight dips (that is the growth rules' job). If no weight has been recorded since day 7 or earlier, the result is 'not enough data', not a flag and not an all-clear. Start age from source; upper bound is this file's choice. Population: healthy term newborns. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Faltering growth: recognition and management of faltering growth in children (NG75)

notes: NICE NG75 rec 1.1.4: consider referral if not returned to birth weight by 3 weeks of age. Firm flag. Metric: the baby's age in completed days while no weight recorded since birth has reached birth weight. Flags at 21 completed days or more (op gte). Once any weight at or above birth weight is recorded the metric is undefined and the rule does not fire, even if a later weight dips (that is the growth rules' job). If no weight has been recorded since day 14 or earlier, the result is 'not enough data', not a flag and not an all-clear. Start age from source; upper bound is this file's choice. Population: healthy term newborns. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Weight Change Nomograms for the First Month After Birth (Paul et al., Pediatrics 2016;138:e20162625)

notes: Paul 2016: among vaginally delivered singletons born at >=36 weeks (2000-5000 g at birth), 14% and 5% were not back to birth weight by 14 and 21 days; cesarean 24% and 8%. 50% at or above birth weight by day 9 (vaginal) and 10 (cesarean). The abstract does not restrict the cohort to exclusive breastfeeding. Kaiser Permanente Northern California, 2009-2013.

source.title: WHO Child Growth Standards: weight velocity, 1-month increments, boys (percentiles)

notes: WHO weight-velocity standard, 1-month increment for interval 0-4w: 5th percentile 460 g, median 1023 g. Measurement interval: weights at day 0 and day 28 (months converted at 30.4375 days and rounded). The engine needs a weight within 3 days of each end; it does not interpolate or rescale increments to other intervals, and otherwise reports 'not enough data'. Evaluated once the interval has ended, for 14 days (this file's choice). Using the 5th percentile as a 'mention it at the next visit' flag is an application policy; the WHO tables describe the distribution and do not prescribe that action. Population: WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study, healthy term breastfed infants.

notes: CDC recommends WHO standards for children <24 months with cutoffs at 2 SD (2.3rd and 97.7th percentiles, often labeled 2nd/98th). CDC 'Using the WHO Growth Standard Charts' (2024) confirms. source.title: Use of World Health Organization and CDC Growth Charts for Children Aged 0-59 Months in the United States (MMWR Recomm Rep 59(RR-9))

notes: CDC: the +2 SD (97.7th percentile) cutoff on WHO charts for <24 months is used to screen high weight-for-length, not weight-for-age. High weight-for-age alone does not indicate excess weight. Informational only; a weight-for-length rule needs length measurements, which are outside v1. Population: healthy infants <24 months.

source.title: Undernutrition

notes: AAP 'Undernutrition': assess when rate of weight gain declines across 2 major percentiles (e.g., 90th, 75th, 25th). Major lines on WHO charts as printed by CDC: 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75, 90, 95, 98. Start at day 14 (this file's choice) because early physiological loss is covered by other entries. Population: healthy term infants (any feeding method unless stated). Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

notes: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.1: concern when current weight is below the 2nd centile for age, whatever the birth weight. Close to CDC's 2.3rd percentile cutoff. Population: healthy term infants (any feeding method unless stated). Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

notes: ABM #3 Table 2, average reported colostrum intake per feed at 0-24 h: 2-10 mL. Observed averages, not prescribed amounts; also a sanity range for supplement volumes. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: ABM Clinical Protocol #3: Supplementary Feedings in the Healthy Term Breastfed Neonate, Revised 2017 (Breastfeed Med 2017;12:188-198, PMID 28294631)

notes: ABM #3 Table 2, average reported colostrum intake per feed at 24-48 h: 5-15 mL. Observed averages, not prescribed amounts; also a sanity range for supplement volumes. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: ABM Clinical Protocol #3: Supplementary Feedings in the Healthy Term Breastfed Neonate, Revised 2017 (Breastfeed Med 2017;12:188-198, PMID 28294631)

notes: ABM #3 Table 2, average reported colostrum intake per feed at 48-72 h: 15-30 mL. Observed averages, not prescribed amounts; also a sanity range for supplement volumes. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: ABM Clinical Protocol #3: Supplementary Feedings in the Healthy Term Breastfed Neonate, Revised 2017 (Breastfeed Med 2017;12:188-198, PMID 28294631)

notes: ABM #3 Table 2, average reported colostrum intake per feed at 72-96 h: 30-60 mL. Observed averages, not prescribed amounts; also a sanity range for supplement volumes. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Colostrum ingested during the first day of life by exclusively breastfed healthy newborn infants (Santoro et al., J Pediatr 2010;156:29-32)

notes: Santoro 2010: mean gain per feed 1.5 +/- 1.1 g on day 1; daily intake 15 +/- 11 g (1 g ~ 1 mL). Real day-1 intake is often below ABM's 2-10 mL. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Neonatal stomach volume and physiology suggest feeding at 1-h intervals (Bergman, Acta Paediatr 2013;102:773-7)

notes: Bergman 2013: 'A stomach capacity of 20 mL translates to a feeding interval of approximately 1 h for a term neonate.' Single-author review of six studies; context only. Population: healthy term infants (any feeding method unless stated). Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Studies in human lactation: milk volumes in lactating women during the onset of lactation and full lactation (Neville et al., Am J Clin Nutr 1988;48:1375-86)

notes: Neville 1988: 498 +/- 129 g/day on day 5; 753 +/- 89 g/day at months 3-5 (test weighing, 13 women; g ~ mL). Disputed vs Kent 2016 pooled 415 +/- 123 g on day 5. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Breastmilk Production in the First 4 Weeks after Birth of Term Infants (Kent, Gardner & Geddes, Nutrients 2016;8:756)

notes: Kent 2016 introduction: day-5 milk transfer of 415 +/- 123 g pooled from seven earlier studies (305 mothers in total); a separate cited study of 10 mothers gives 653 +/- 154 g in week 2. These are not Kent 2016's own convenience sample, which recruited mothers with breastfeeding difficulties. Population: breastfeeding mothers of term infants in the cited studies. Disputed vs Neville 1988 (498 g).

source.title: Review citing Kent et al. 2006 (Pediatrics 117:e387) for 24-h intake range

notes: Kent 2006 (exclusive breastfeeding, 1-6 months, 71 dyads): mean 788 +/- 169 g/24 h, range 478-1356 g. Verified via a PMC review citing Kent 2006; the Kent abstract does not state the 24-h total and the full text was 403. WHO-commissioned meta-analysis (Rios-Leyvraz 2023): means 624 mL/day at 1 month, 735 at 3 months, 729 at 6 months. Range of normal is wide; do not flag on intake alone. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: The Volume of Breast Milk Intake in Infants and Young Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Rios-Leyvraz & Yao, Breastfeed Med 2023)

notes: Rios-Leyvraz & Yao 2023 meta-analysis, subgroup of healthy term infants exclusively breastfed through 6 months: 624 mL/day at 1 month, 735 at 3 months, 729 at 6 months. Deuterium dilution gave higher estimates than test weighing. Population: healthy term, exclusively breastfed.

source.title: Volume and frequency of breastfeedings and fat content of breast milk throughout the day (Kent et al., Pediatrics 2006;117:e387-95)

notes: Kent 2006: a breastfeed averaged 76.0 +/- 12.6 g (range 0-240 g), i.e. 67% of milk available in the breast. Single feeds vary widely; never flag a single feed. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: How Often and How Much Should Your Baby Eat?

notes: AAP 2024: 'Most breastfed infants take 1 oz in the first few weeks' (~30 mL), topping out at roughly 4.5 oz (~133 mL) at a year. Approximate. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Quantifying breast milk intake by term and preterm infants for input into paediatric physiologically based pharmacokinetic models (Yeung et al., Matern Child Nutr 2020;16:e12938)

notes: Yeung 2020: 'The daily milk intake volume of 150 ml/kg is commonly used'; fitted maximum 152.6 mL/kg/day at ~20 days, declining afterwards (roughly ~100 mL/kg/day by 6 months per the fitted model; not stated directly). No allowed source found stating a 150-200 mL/kg/day range for healthy term infants (that range appears in preterm literature). Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: How Often and How Much Should Your Baby Eat?

notes: AAP 2024: 'Babies might only take in half ounce per feeding for the first day or two of life' (~15 mL), then 1-2 oz. Disputed with CDC/AAP 2022 (1-2 oz from the first days). Population: healthy term infants, formula-fed. Excludes preterm and medically complex infants, and specialized formulas.

source.title: Amount and Schedule of Baby Formula Feedings

notes: AAP 2022: 'In the first week after birth, babies should be eating no more than about 1 to 2 ounces (30 to 60 ml) per feed.' CDC 2026: offer 1-2 oz every 2-3 h in the first days. Disputed: an AAP 2018 Q&A page says 2-3 oz in the first few days. Soft flag (possible overfeeding), not urgent. Population: healthy term infants, formula-fed. Excludes preterm and medically complex infants, and specialized formulas.

source.title: Amount and Schedule of Baby Formula Feedings

notes: AAP 2022: through the first month babies take 3-4 oz (90-120 mL) per feed, about every 3-4 hours by end of month 1. Population: healthy term infants, formula-fed. Excludes preterm and medically complex infants, and specialized formulas. Age window is this file's choice.

source.title: Amount and Schedule of Baby Formula Feedings

notes: AAP 2022: at 6 months, 6-8 oz (180-240 mL) at each of 4 or 5 feedings in 24 hours. Population: healthy term infants, formula-fed. Excludes preterm and medically complex infants, and specialized formulas. Age window is this file's choice.

source.title: Amount and Schedule of Baby Formula Feedings

notes: AAP 2022: about 2.5 oz (75 mL) per pound (453 g) of body weight per day = ~165 mL/kg/day. Average guide; individual needs vary. Population: healthy term infants, formula-fed. Excludes preterm and medically complex infants, and specialized formulas.

source.title: Amount and Schedule of Baby Formula Feedings

notes: AAP 2022: 'no more than an average of about 32 ounces (960 mL) of formula in 24 hours' (exact conversion is 946 mL; page states 960). CDC uses 32 oz only as a vitamin D cutoff, not as a cap. Soft flag; sustained intake above this is worth discussing. Population: healthy term infants, formula-fed. Excludes preterm and medically complex infants, and specialized formulas.

source.title: How Much and How Often to Breastfeed

notes: CDC 2026: 'Your baby will breastfeed about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours'; newborns may feed every 1-3 hours. Fewer than 8 in the first weeks -> flag. Upper bound 28 days is this file's choice. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: How Often To Breastfeed

notes: AAP 2015: 'be sure he receives eight to twelve feedings in every twenty-four-hour period' in the early weeks. Page dated 2015. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: How Often and How Much Should Your Baby Eat?

notes: AAP 2024: newborns nurse about every 2 hours; '10-12 sessions in 24 hours is the norm.' Disputed vs 8-12 (CDC, AAP 2015). Informational only. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: How Often To Breastfeed

notes: AAP 2015: 'He should not go longer than about two to three hours during the day or four hours at night without a feeding' (early weeks). Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: How Often To Breastfeed

notes: AAP 2015: no longer than about four hours at night without a feeding in the early weeks. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: Volume and frequency of breastfeedings and fat content of breast milk throughout the day (Kent et al., Pediatrics 2006;117:e387-95)

notes: Kent 2006: infants breastfed 11 +/- 3 times in 24 hours (range 6-18) at 1-6 months. Exclusively breastfed, 71 dyads, Australia. Population: healthy term newborns, breastfed. Excludes preterm, NICU, and medically complex infants.

source.title: How Often and How Much Should Your Baby Eat?

notes: AAP 2024: 'If bottle-fed, most newborns eat every 2 to 3 hours; 8 times is generally recommended as the minimum every 24 hours.' CDC: formula-fed newborns feed 8-12 times in 24 h. Population: healthy term infants, formula-fed. Excludes preterm and medically complex infants, and specialized formulas.

source.title: Amount and Schedule of Baby Formula Feedings

notes: AAP 2022: 4 or 5 feedings of 6-8 oz at 6 months. CDC 2026: 5-6 times per 24 h at 6-12 months. Disputed slightly; informational. Population: healthy term infants, formula-fed. Excludes preterm and medically complex infants, and specialized formulas.

source.title: Accuracy and precision of test weighing to assess milk intake in newborn infants (Savenije & Brand, Arch Dis Child Fetal Neonatal Ed 2006)

notes: Savenije & Brand 2006: routine single test weighing in 94 newborns fed by bottle, cup or tube (true intake known) had mean bias 1.3 mL and 95% limits of agreement about -12 to +15 mL; the authors advised against clinical use of single test weights. These are method-agreement limits for that setting, not a validated uncertainty for home scales, other ages, feed sizes or techniques. Do not display them as an error bar; a home uncertainty model is deferred until validated.

source.title: The development of an accurate test weighing technique for preterm and high-risk hospitalized infants (Haase et al., Breastfeed Med 2009)

notes: Haase 2009: with a standardized technique only one measure was outside the clinically acceptable +/-5 g (r^2=0.998). Kinoshita 2025: mean absolute error 1.7 +/- 2.2 g with duplicate pre/post weights. Population: hospitalized preterm/high-risk infants on clinical-grade scales; accuracy has only been validated in preterm infants (Esquerra-Zwiers 2024).

source.title: Comparison of human milk bottle with infant/toddler test weights in the community setting (Esquerra-Zwiers et al., BMC Nutr 2024)

notes: Esquerra-Zwiers 2024: parents performed test weights on infants and toddlers under 2 years in a community setting (31 participants, 101 paired measurements, mostly older infants), using a specific scale (Tanita BD-815U: 2 g up to 6 kg, 5 g from 6-15 kg) and protocol with researchers present. The scale's resolution describes that study, not a minimum the app can require. Results do not extend to unsupervised newborn breastfeeds.

source.title: Human Milk Oligosaccharides and Bacterial Profile Modulate Infant Body Composition during Exclusive Breastfeeding (Cheema et al., Int J Mol Sci 2022;23:2865)

notes: Human milk density ~1.03 g/mL (Cheema 2022); Esquerra-Zwiers 2024 measured specific gravity 1.034. Treating 1 g as 1 mL overstates volume ~3%; divide grams by 1.03 for mL.

source.title: Breast Milk Intake from 1 to 8.5 Months of Lactation in the Multisite Mothers, Infants and Lactation Quality (MILQ) study (Moore et al., Adv Nutr 2025)

notes: MILQ 2025 corrected test-weighing volumes by a factor of 1.05 for insensible water loss within its research protocol. Arthur 1987 (PMID 3694369) found evaporative loss during feeds. A protocol-specific correction, not a mandatory correction for every home feed. Age window is this file's choice.

source.title: Validity of a 3-Hour Breast Milk Expression Protocol in Estimating Current Maternal Milk Production Capacity and Infant Breast Milk Intake (Roznowski et al., Breastfeed Med 2020)

notes: Roznowski 2020: the gold standard for milk production is 2-4 days of 24-hour infant intake test-weighing. A single feed or partial day is not a supply measure. Day-to-day within-mother CV ~8.9% (Dewey 1991).

source.title: Volume and frequency of breastfeedings and fat content of breast milk throughout the day (Kent et al., Pediatrics 2006;117:e387-95)

notes: Kent 2006: a breastfeed removed 67.3 +/- 7.8% (range 0-100%) of milk available in the breast; residual milk is normal. Exclusively breastfed, 1-6 months.

source.title: Importance of vacuum for breastmilk expression (Kent et al., Breastfeed Med 2008)

notes: Kent 2008: pumping at maximum comfortable vacuum removed 65.5 +/- 4.1% of available milk (118.5 mL); lower vacuum removed less. Pump output depends on pump, vacuum and fullness, so it is not a fixed fraction of supply. Age window is this file's choice.

source.title: Validity of a 3-Hour Breast Milk Expression Protocol in Estimating Current Maternal Milk Production Capacity and Infant Breast Milk Intake (Roznowski et al., Breastfeed Med 2020)

notes: Roznowski 2020: in 16 paired measurements (23 enrolled), a 3-hour pumping protocol estimated 1,085 +/- 300 g/24 h vs 717 +/- 119 g/24 h infant intake by test weighing (~day 54). Valid for production capacity but not for infant intake. Exclusively breastfeeding mothers of term singletons, 4-10 weeks postpartum. Window is this file's choice.

source.title: Maternal versus infant factors related to breast milk intake and residual milk volume: the DARLING study (Dewey et al., Pediatrics 1991)

notes: Dewey 1991 (DARLING), measured at 3 months only: intake 818, volume extracted 914, residual milk 109 g/day (residual = extracted by expression on a separate day minus test-weighed intake); day-to-day CV ~8.9%. 73 exclusively breastfed infants. Applying it beyond 3 months is this file's choice.

source.title: Milk Volume at 2 Weeks Predicts Mother's Own Milk Feeding at Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Discharge for Very Low Birthweight Infants (Hoban et al., Breastfeed Med 2018)

notes: Hoban 2018: pumped mother's own milk >=500 mL/day at 2 weeks predicts milk feeding at NICU discharge (VLBW infants). Canadian Paediatric Society 2023 and Meier 2017 use the same target. Population: pump-dependent mothers of very low birthweight NICU infants ONLY. Do not apply to term breastfed babies; recorded for completeness.

source.title: Defining Low Milk Supply: A Data-Driven Diagnostic Framework and Risk Factor Analysis for Breastfeeding Women (Jin et al., Nutrients 2025)

notes: Jin 2025: data-driven low-supply cutoff 708 mL/24 h milk production (AUC 0.92) or 694 mL/24 h infant intake; mothers 4-26 weeks postpartum, n=460, Australia. Low confidence: single cohort, not replicated, not a guideline, and requires complete 24-h test weighing. Do NOT use for flags; see 'Milk-supply estimate: evidence' in docs/CLINICAL_REFERENCE.md.
